J. Jones , Yu Yuan , Sergio Maffeis View a PDF of the paper titled Speedbumps: Rejection Attacks on Speculative Decoding, by Adam Y. J. Jones and 2 other authors View PDF HTML (experimental) Abstract: Speculative decoding is a popular technique for increasing the speed and reducing the costs of large language model (LLM) inference by verifying multiple draft tokens in a single target-model forward pass. The resulting benefit depends on the ability of the drafter to approximate the target model's distribution. In this work, we study Speculative Rejection Attacks (SRAs), a novel class of attacks that cause draft and target models to disagree more often, resulting in fewer draft tokens being accepted per draft cycle. This leads to more target model forward passes needed per generated token, slowing down inference and increasing costs for the victim. We introduce two attacks which append an adversarial suffix to attacker-controlled content to degrade speculative decoding on a victim's prompts. Both attacks optimise the expected length of the accepted speculative prefix, estimating per-depth acceptance from the target's probability of the drafted proposals (Speedbump-P) or from the overlap between the draft and target distributions (Speedbump-D). In some cases, attacks degrade speculative decoding to the point of being slower than autoregressive decoding. The degradation reduces the output quality - regularisation restores output quality but gives up most of the degradation, trading effectiveness for stealthiness. Additionally, the suffixes remain effective under sampling, and transfer across drafters (Speedbump-P) or across target models sharing a drafter (Speedbump-D). These findings identify the draft-target interaction of speculative decoding as a realistic attack surface through which adversarial inputs can inflate inference costs. selected_records.title: Speedbumps: Rejection Attacks on Speculative Decoding

article.body:
Researchers outline attacks that can slow speculative decoding

A paper submitted to arXiv on Oct. 7 describes two attacks that append adversarial suffixes to attacker-controlled content to make large language model speculative decoding less efficient, increasing inference time and cost for a victim.

The authors, Adam Y. J. Jones, Yu Yuan and Sergio Maffeis, call the approach Speculative Rejection Attacks. Their paper, “Speedbumps: Rejection Attacks on Speculative Decoding,” says the attacks increase disagreement between a draft model and a target model, so fewer proposed tokens are accepted in each decoding cycle.

Speculative decoding speeds generation by having a drafter propose multiple tokens, which the target model then verifies in a single forward pass. The efficiency gain depends on how closely the drafter approximates the target model’s distribution, the paper says. When proposals are rejected more often, the target must make more forward passes per generated token.

The two methods optimise the expected length of the accepted speculative prefix in different ways. Speedbump-P estimates acceptance at each depth using the target model’s probability for drafted proposals; Speedbump-D uses the overlap between the draft and target distributions, according to the paper’s abstract.

The authors report that, in some cases, the attacks reduced speculative decoding’s speed to below that of autoregressive decoding. They also say the suffixes remained effective under sampling, with Speedbump-P transferring across drafters and Speedbump-D across target models that share a drafter.

The paper reports a trade-off: the degradation can reduce output quality, while regularisation can restore quality but gives up most of the attack’s effect. The authors describe this as a balance between effectiveness and stealthiness.

The work identifies interactions between draft and target models as a potential route for adversarial inputs to raise inference costs. The arXiv abstract does not provide specific performance figures or describe a deployment against a live service.
